rationale: Kālidāsa’s authorship of the Raghuvaṃśa is unquestioned in the commentarial tradition and in modern scholarship.

sources.quote: vṛttaṃ rāmasya vālmīkeḥ kṛtis tau kiṃnarasvanau

rationale: Raghuvaṃśa 15.63–64 names Vālmīki’s Rāmāyaṇa (“prācetasopajñaṃ rāmāyaṇam”) as the song of Kuśa and Lava; cantos 10–15 follow Vālmīki’s plot in abridged form.
The poem names the Rāmāyaṇa and its author Prācetasa (Vālmīki).

sources.quote: anindyā nandinī nāma dhenur āvavṛte vanāt

qualifiers.role: sage who shelters the abandoned Sītā

qualifiers.note: 14.31–80 (abandonment) and 15.81–84 (entry into the earth), following Vālmīki

sources.quote: sā sītām aṅkam āropya bhartari prahitekṣaṇām
geye kena vinītau vāṃ kasya ceyaṃ kaveḥ kṛtiḥ

qualifiers.note: Vālmīki: son of Nābhāga; Raghuvaṃśa: son of Raghu

rationale: Raghuvaṃśa cantos 5–8 make Aja Raghu’s son.
competing: VR (CE) 1.69.30 makes Aja the son of Nābhāga.

sources.quote: kumāraḥ śabdavedhīti mayā pāpam idaṃ kṛtam

qualifiers.note: the curse is fulfilled when Daśaratha dies of grief for Rāma

rationale: Cantos 1–8 are accepted as Kālidāsa’s; cantos 9–17 are generally held to be by another hand.

sources.quote: tāvat sa vahnir bhavanetrajanmā bhasmāvaśeṣaṃ madanaṃ cakāra
iyeṣa sā kartum avandhyarūpatāṃ samādhim āsthāya tapobhir ātmanaḥ

qualifiers.note: only in the continuation cantos 9–17; the authentic cantos 1–8 end before the birth

rationale: The title announces Kumāra’s birth, but the eight cantos generally accepted as Kālidāsa’s stop at the wedding night (Ks 8.91).
The prologue names the play as “composed by Kālidāsa”.
The characters, the hermitage union, the rejection at court and the naming of Bharata follow MBh (CE) 1.62–69; the curse and the ring are Kālidāsa’s additions (see cmp:shakuntala-ring-curse).
Absent from MBh (CE) 1.62–69.

qualifiers.note: the curse explains the rejection scene within the larger story

rationale: Not a retelling: the poem alludes to the Rāmāyaṇa (Sītā, Rāma’s footprints, Hanumān as messenger) to model its own separation and message.
“Son of the Wind” (pavanatanaya) is Hanumān; the verse compares the cloud to him.

qualifiers.role: the yakṣa’s master (dhanapati), whose anger exiled him

rationale: One of Kālidāsa’s three plays; his authorship is not disputed.
The play dramatises the Purūravas–Urvaśī story known from RV 10.95 and ŚB 11.5.1, ending happily with Indra’s permission for Urvaśī to remain with the king.
competing: Kālidāsa’s immediate source is debated: the Matsya Purāṇa (chs. 24) and Viṣṇu Purāṇa versions are candidates, and some scholars think the Purāṇic versions postdate the play.

rationale: Attributed to Bhāsa by Gaṇapati Śāstrī with the rest of the Trivandrum corpus; the plays themselves name no author.

rationale: The plays open with the stage-direction “after the nāndī the sūtradhāra enters”, which Gaṇapati Śāstrī read as the feature Bāṇa ascribes to Bhāsa’s plays (“sūtradhārakṛtārambhair nāṭakaiḥ”, Harṣacarita intro v. 15).
competing: The same convention occurs in other Kerala play manuscripts, so it may reflect Kerala stage practice rather than Bhāsa (Tieken 1993).

rationale: Later critics ascribe a Svapnavāsavadatta to Bhāsa, and the Trivandrum play of that name matches several of their descriptions.
competing: Some verses quoted from Bhāsa’s Svapnavāsavadatta are not found in the Trivandrum text.

rationale: Follows the Rāma story from the exile to the coronation, with major inventions (the statue-house; Kaikeyī’s motive tied to a curse).
Covers Kiṣkindhā to Yuddha (Vālin’s death to Rāma’s consecration), closely following Vālmīki’s order of events.

rationale: The gift of armour and earrings to Indra comes from MBh 3.294; the play moves it to the battlefield and changes the terms (see cmp:karna-armour-gift).
Presupposes Bhīma’s union with Hiḍimbā and Ghaṭotkaca’s birth (MBh 1.143); the encounter itself is invented.
Act 1 dramatises the birth and the transfer to Vraja.
